newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD seeks new innovative image.
newsitem.headline: German SPD seeks new innovative image.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), bidding to oust Christian Democrat Chancellor Helmut Kohl next year, on Wednesday held a special "innovation congress" to present themselves as a party ready for change in the style of Britain's Labour Party.

The SPD, whose fractious pressure groups long opposed many forms of modern technology, openly embraced biotechnology and genetic engineering as ways to create jobs and defend Germany's economic competitiveness in a globalising world.

But the two-day congress in Duesseldorf, highlighted by a solid morning of long speeches by the party's leading lights to assembled business and trade union leaders, lacked the spark which helped sweep Tony Blair's "new Labour" to power in Britain on May 1.

SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine and his main rival, Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder, carefully avoided the unresolved issue of who should lead the party's challenge against Kohl in elections in September 1998.
"More and more people are putting their hopes and expectations in the Social Democrats, not just in England, but also in Germany," Schroeder, a charismatic pro-business leader, told the congress.
"The only way to stay competitive and ensure the prosperity of a wide section of the working population is a comprehensive modernisation of the economy and society," he said.
Like Blair, the SPD speakers also stressed the need for better education and vocational training and pledged support for young entrepreneurs at the cutting edge of technology.
Since the landslide victory of Britain's revamped Labour party, the SPD, in opposition for over 14 years, has sought ways to follow Labour's example.
North Rhine-Westphalia premier Johannes Rau said people wanted to feel "a fresh wind in Germany".

But the fractious party still has to win over influential pressure groups which have long opposed modern technology and pro-business reforms. Many of the SPD's leaders come from the same 1960s student circles as their internal critics.
Lafontaine apparently had them in mind when he said: "We must overcome fear of the future to achieve more freedom and prosperity."

Wolfgang Clement, North Rhine-Westphalia state economics minister and a leading pro-business figure in the SPD, assured the audience the party did not want to swap Germany's welfare state for Thatcherite reforms.
"Rhineland capitalism can be modern," he said, using a term for Germany's so-called social market economy, "it can be just as in step with the times as its Anglo-Saxon counterpart."
Politicians from Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said the meeting's glossy innovation manifesto was full of empty words and challenged the party to act.
"The SPD is trying to tell citizens a fairy tale about how much they like innovation. But words and deeds are far apart in the SPD," CDU secretary general Peter Hintze said.

Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers accused the SPD of blocking innovative government plans including tax reforms, deregulation of communication services, biotechnology research and the Transrapid high-speed magnetic levitation train.
It was not clear whether SPD members shared the party leaders' optimism about the country's ability to reform to encourage innovation.
"In England whatever is not prohibited is allowed. But in Germany whatever is not expressly allowed is prohibited," one party member said at an open discussion at the congress.
